title: Explain how you secure a banking REST API using OAuth2 and JWT — the token flow, signature validation, access versus refresh tokens — and how you defend against the OWASP top risks such as SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, IDOR, and broken authentication.
topicTitle: Explain how you secure a banking REST API using OAuth2 and JWT

s1_definition.profdef: OAuth2 is an authorization framework in which an authorization server issues access tokens that a client presents to protected resources. JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, digitally signed token format carrying claims such as the subject and roles; it is signed by the authorization server (for example with RS256) so any service can verify it using the public key without a shared secret. A short-lived access token authorizes individual requests, while a longer-lived refresh token obtains new access tokens without re-prompting the user. OWASP publishes the top web application security risks, and a secure banking API defends against them with parameterized queries, output encoding, stateless CSRF handling, per-user query scoping, and strong password hashing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants to use services inside National Bank of India. He shows his ID once at the security desk (the authorization server), and they hand him a tamper-proof wristband (the JWT access token) stamped with his name and what he is allowed to do, valid for only fifteen minutes. Every department he visits just glances at the wristband's official hologram (the signature) and lets him in — they do not need to call the security desk again. When the wristband expires, he uses a special renewal card (the refresh token) to get a fresh wristband without showing his ID all over again. OWASP is the bank's list of common robbery tricks, and the security team has a specific countermeasure for each one.
s1_definition.oneliner: OAuth2 issues a signed, short-lived JWT the client carries on every request, services verify its signature with a public key, and each OWASP risk has a specific defense you apply by default.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OAuth2 is an authorization framework in which an authorization server issues access tokens that a client presents to protected resources. JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, digitally signed token format carrying claims such as the subject and roles; it is signed by the authorization server (for example with RS256) so any service can verify it using the public key without a shared secret. A short-lived access token authorizes individual requests, while a longer-lived refresh token obtains new access tokens without re-prompting the user. OWASP publishes the top web application security risks, and a secure banking API defends against them with parameterized queries, output encoding, stateless CSRF handling, per-user query scoping, and strong password hashing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh wants to use services inside National Bank of India. He shows his ID once at the security desk (the authorization server), and they hand him a tamper-proof wristband (the JWT access token) stamped with his name and what he is allowed to do, valid for only fifteen minutes. Every department he visits just glances at the wristband's official hologram (the signature) and lets him in — they do not need to call the security desk again. When the wristband expires, he uses a special renewal card (the refresh token) to get a fresh wristband without showing his ID all over again. OWASP is the bank's list of common robbery tricks, and the security team has a specific countermeasure for each one.

**One line to remember:** OAuth2 issues a signed, short-lived JWT the client carries on every request, services verify its signature with a public key, and each OWASP risk has a specific defense you apply by default.

sections.s2_technical:
The JWT and OAuth2 flow starts when the client sends credentials to the authorization server, for example `POST /token` with a username and password to a server like Keycloak. The authorization server validates the credentials and returns a JWT signed with RS256, a private-public key pair. The token has three parts separated by dots: a header describing the algorithm, a payload carrying claims such as the subject `"rajesh"`, the roles `["USER"]`, and an expiry timestamp, and a signature. For example the payload decodes to something like `{"sub":"rajesh","roles":["USER"],"exp":1730000000}`.

On every subsequent request the client sends the token in the Authorization header: `GET /accounts` with `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`. The API gateway or resource server validates the signature using the authorization server's public key, fetched from a JWKS endpoint. Because the signature is verified with a public key, no service needs the private key or a shared secret, which is what makes JWT stateless and horizontally scalable. If the token is valid the request is forwarded with the claims available; if it is expired, the client uses its refresh token to get a new access token. Keeping access tokens short-lived (around fifteen minutes) limits the damage if one is stolen, while the refresh token can be revoked server-side.

For the OWASP risks, each has a concrete code-level defense. SQL injection is prevented by parameterized queries; with Spring Data JPA this happens automatically because it binds parameters rather than concatenating strings, so `repository.findByAccountId(id)` is safe. Cross-site scripting, or XSS, is prevented by encoding output and setting a Content-Security-Policy header so injected scripts cannot run in the browser. Cross-site request forgery, or CSRF, is disabled for stateless JWT APIs because there is no session cookie the browser would attach automatically; CSRF only matters when authentication rides on cookies. Insecure Direct Object Reference, or IDOR, is the dangerous case where Rajesh requests `/accounts/CUR3001` and sees Priya's account; the defense is to scope every query to the authenticated user, for example `WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = :currentUser`, so a user can never read a record they do not own. Broken authentication is defended with BCrypt password hashing (which is slow and salted on purpose), short-lived tokens, and token rotation.

A senior-level nuance: never trust claims blindly. Validate the token's signature, issuer, audience, and expiry on every request, and for sensitive operations like a large transfer, re-check authorization at the service layer rather than relying only on the gateway. Defense in depth means the service itself scopes the query to the caller even if the gateway already authenticated them.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, customers call an API to view their own account. We must make sure a logged-in user can only ever see their own data, that passwords are stored safely, and that the queries cannot be tricked.

Problem 1 — Rajesh logs in and the system must prove who he is on every later request without asking for his password again. This is exactly what a JWT access token does: he logs in once, receives a signed token, and presents it on each call; the service verifies the signature and trusts the claims.

Problem 2 — Rajesh (SAV2001) tries to fetch Priya's account (CUR3001) by changing the id in the URL. This is exactly the IDOR vulnerability, and the defense is scoping every lookup to the authenticated user so the service refuses to return an account the caller does not own.

Problem 3 — The bank must never store raw passwords, because a database leak would expose every customer. This is exactly why we hash passwords with BCrypt, a deliberately slow, salted algorithm, so even a stolen database does not reveal the actual passwords.

The code will contain an `Account` class, a simple `TokenService` that issues and validates a signed token (a readable stand-in for a real JWT library), a `PasswordHasher` using a salted hash, and an `AccountSecurityService` whose `getAccount` method enforces that the caller can only read their own account. A `SecurityDemo` main class shows Rajesh succeeding on his own account and being denied Priya's.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh with username "rajesh" and password "rajesh@Secure1" owning SAV2001 (Rs.1,000,000), Priya owning CUR3001 (Rs.250,000), a signing key, and a 15-minute access token.

Step 1: The hasher takes Rajesh's raw password, generates a random salt, combines salt and password, and produces a one-way hash stored as salt-colon-hash. The raw password is never stored. A correct login re-hashes with the same salt and matches; a wrong password produces a different hash and fails.

Step 2: The demo builds the account map where each account records its owner username. SAV2001 is owned by "rajesh" and CUR3001 by "priya".

Step 3: The token service issues Rajesh a token containing the payload "rajesh" plus an expiry timestamp 900 seconds in the future, followed by a signature computed over that payload. The whole thing is Base64-encoded into the bearer token.

Step 4: Rajesh calls `getAccount(token, "SAV2001")`. The service validates the token: it recomputes the signature and confirms it matches, and checks the expiry is in the future, then extracts the caller "rajesh". It looks up SAV2001, sees its owner is "rajesh" which equals the caller, logs GRANTED, and returns the account so Rajesh sees his Rs.1,000,000 balance.

Step 5: Rajesh then calls `getAccount(token, "CUR3001")`, an IDOR attempt. The token still validates to "rajesh", but CUR3001's owner is "priya", which does not equal the caller. The service logs DENIED and throws a SecurityException, so Rajesh never sees Priya's balance.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  1. Client → Auth Server: POST /token {username:"rajesh", password}
       │ validate credentials (BCrypt match)
       ▼
  2. Auth Server → Client: JWT (RS256 signed)
       header.{sub:"rajesh", roles:["USER"], exp:+15min}.signature
       │
       ▼
  3. Client → API: GET /accounts/SAV2001
       Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
       │
       ▼
  4. API Gateway / Resource Server
       │ validate signature (JWKS public key)
       │ check issuer, audience, expiry ✓
       ▼
  5. AccountSecurityService.getAccount(token, "SAV2001")
       │ caller = "rajesh"
       │ account SAV2001 owner = "rajesh"
       ├─ owner == caller ──→ GRANTED → return balance Rs.1,000,000
       │
       └─ IDOR path: getAccount(token, "CUR3001")
             │ account CUR3001 owner = "priya" ≠ "rajesh"
             ▼
           DENIED → SecurityException → 403 Forbidden

  OWASP defenses applied:
    SQLi  → parameterized queries (JPA binds params)
    XSS   → output encoding + CSP header
    CSRF  → disabled for stateless JWT (no session cookie)
    IDOR  → WHERE id=? AND owner=:caller (scope every query)
    Auth  → BCrypt hash + short-lived token + rotation
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To secure a banking API I use OAuth2 for authorization and JWT for the token format. The flow starts when the client sends credentials to an authorization server like Keycloak, which validates them and returns a JWT signed with RS256. The token carries claims such as the subject and the user's roles along with a short expiry, typically fifteen minutes. On every later request the client sends the token in the Authorization header as a bearer token, and each service validates the signature using the authorization server's public key from its JWKS endpoint. Because verification uses a public key, services do not share secrets and the system scales horizontally. When the access token expires, the client uses a longer-lived refresh token to get a new one without logging in again, and that refresh token can be revoked server-side if a device is lost.

The most important security habit I apply is scoping every query to the authenticated user. In my banking work, the classic mistake is Insecure Direct Object Reference, where a user changes an account id in the URL and sees someone else's account. I defend against it by always adding the owner condition to the query, so a user physically cannot read a record they do not own, and I enforce this at the service layer as defense in depth even when the gateway already authenticated the request.

For the other OWASP risks, I rely on specific defenses. SQL injection is prevented because Spring Data JPA uses parameterized queries that bind values rather than concatenating strings. Cross-site scripting is handled with output encoding and a Content-Security-Policy header. Cross-site request forgery protection is actually disabled for stateless JWT APIs because there is no session cookie the browser would automatically attach, so the attack does not apply. Broken authentication is addressed with BCrypt password hashing, which is deliberately slow and salted, so even a database leak does not expose real passwords.

In my mini-project I demonstrated all of this concretely: passwords stored only as salted one-way hashes, a signed token that the service validates for both signature and expiry on every call, and an account service that grants Rajesh access to his own account but throws a security exception and logs the denial when he tries to read Priya's account. That combination of authentication, per-user authorization, parameterized data access, and strong password storage is what I mean when I say a banking API is secure by default rather than as an afterthought.
